title: Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE): A Protocol for Network Address Translator (NAT) Traversal
summary: Describes ICE, a protocol for NAT traversal in UDP-based communication. Endpoints gather candidate addresses, using STUN and TURN, and test which pairs actually connect. This document obsoletes RFC 5245.

plainLanguage.summary: Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) helps two peers find a working UDP path through networks that may use address translators. They exchange candidate addresses, test pairs with STUN and select a pair that works.

subtitle: ICE tests possible UDP address pairs and selects a working path between peers.

tldr.problem: Peers behind network address translators may not know which addresses and ports can reach one another directly.
tldr.mechanism: Each peer gathers local, translated and relayed candidates, exchanges them, checks candidate pairs with STUN, and nominates a working pair.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8445 obsoletes RFC 5245, removes aggressive nomination and is independent of signaling protocols. It has been updated by RFC 8863.

today: RFC 8445 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5245 and has been updated by RFC 8863.

sections.title: Finding a Path Through NATs
sections.content:
Peers usually exchange IP addresses and ports when setting up a data session. Network Address Translators (NATs) can make those addresses and ports unusable from the other peer's network.

ICE gathers several possible transport addresses, exchanges them through a separate signaling mechanism and tests connectivity between peers. This specification covers UDP-based data streams; it does not establish the signaling connection used to exchange candidates.
sections.plainLanguage: Each peer may have several addresses, and some may not be reachable from the other peer. ICE tests address pairs to find a path that both sides can use.

sections.title: Candidate Types and Priorities
sections.content:
A candidate is a possible transport address consisting of an IP address and port. Host candidates come from local interfaces; server-reflexive candidates show an address mapped by a NAT; relayed candidates use a TURN server; and peer-reflexive candidates can be discovered during checks.

Each candidate has a priority that determines the order of checks. The recommended type preferences favor host candidates, then peer-reflexive and server-reflexive candidates, with relayed candidates as a last resort. Redundant candidates with the same transport address and base can be removed.
sections.plainLanguage: ICE collects addresses from the device, NAT mappings and relay servers. It ranks them so that its checks can try preferred options first.

sections.title: Pairing Candidates and Checking Connectivity
sections.content:
After exchanging candidates, each agent pairs compatible local and remote candidates and sorts the pairs by priority. These ordered pairs form the checklist. A STUN Binding request sent from one candidate toward the other tests whether that pair can carry traffic.

A successful check creates a valid pair. When an agent receives a check, it schedules a triggered check on that pair. If a response reveals a previously unknown mapped address, the agent can add a peer-reflexive candidate. Candidate pairs move through Frozen, Waiting, In-Progress, Succeeded or Failed states.

The default maximum is 100 candidate pairs across the checklist set, and implementations must make this limit configurable.
sections.plainLanguage: Each agent tests candidate pairs with STUN requests and records successful pairs. A working pair can be used for data once the agents select it.

sections.title: Roles and Pair Selection
sections.content:
One agent controls the choice of the final candidate pair; the other waits for that choice. When both agents are full implementations, the initiating agent controls. When one is lite, the full agent controls; a lite agent uses host candidates and responds to checks but does not run the full check process.

The controlling agent waits until checks find a valid pair for each data-stream component, then nominates a pair with the USE-CANDIDATE attribute. Once nomination succeeds for each component, those pairs are selected for data. RFC 8445 removes aggressive nomination from RFC 5245.
sections.plainLanguage: The controlling agent chooses which successful pair to use. Once both agents accept the choice, they send data on the selected pairs.

sections.title: Keepalives, Restarts and Timing
sections.content:
Either agent can restart ICE by providing new candidate information and changing its username fragment and password. The restart clears earlier ICE state, while data may continue over the existing session during the change.

Agents send STUN Binding Indications as keepalives when a selected pair has had no traffic for the configured interval. The recommended interval is 15 seconds and it must not be shorter. Checks and retransmissions are paced; the recommended default Ta is 50 ms, and the retransmission timeout must not be below 500 ms.
sections.plainLanguage: Keepalives help maintain network address bindings when the data stream is quiet. If the connection details change, either agent can restart the candidate checks.

sections.title: Address Privacy and Check Limits
sections.content:
Candidate gathering and exchange can reveal local and public addresses to network observers or signaling participants. The RFC recommends that implementations let users control which network interfaces produce candidates when address privacy matters.

A participant can send many candidates and cause another agent to direct STUN checks toward a target. ICE limits the number of candidate pairs to reduce this amplification risk. Connectivity checks also use short-term credentials exchanged by the agents.
sections.plainLanguage: Candidate lists can reveal addresses, and a participant can try to cause excessive checks. ICE uses credentials and a configurable pair limit to reduce these risks.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 5245
sections.content:
RFC 8445 clarifies the earlier ICE specification and changes procedures based on implementation feedback. It removes SIP and SDP procedures so that the core protocol does not depend on one signaling protocol; separate usage documents describe signaling-specific details.

The update removes aggressive nomination, changes candidate-pair state and check scheduling procedures, revises timing calculations, adds the ice2 option and changes IPv6 guidance.
sections.plainLanguage: This revision makes ICE independent of a specific signaling protocol and changes some check and timing rules. It also removes aggressive nomination.
